title: Italian Grapes Around the World
quiz.0.question: Why do Italian grapes struggle to go global?
quiz.0.options.1: Strong terroir dependence, clonal complexity, a high knowledge barrier, the need for long ageing
quiz.0.explanation: Italian grapes struggle abroad because they are extremely demanding of terroir (hard to replicate away from home), have many very different clones, are little known by consumers, and many need years of ageing (a poor fit for the New World's drink-now market).
quiz.1.question: In which Californian area has Sangiovese been most successful?
quiz.1.explanation: The Atlas Peak area of Napa Valley (high elevation, volcanic soils) is California's most representative Sangiovese area, with conditions closer to Tuscany.
quiz.2.question: According to DNA research, what is Argentina's Bonarda?
quiz.2.explanation: DNA research has shown that Argentina's "Bonarda" is actually Douce Noir from Savoie in France (called Charbono in California) — neither Piemonte's Bonarda nor the Croatina known as Bonarda in Oltrepò Pavese. It is a common name confusion.
quiz.3.question: Which is NOT a key factor in Prosecco's global success?
quiz.3.explanation: Prosecco's success factors: affordable prices, an easy-drinking style (no consumer education needed), a simple name, clear occasions (celebrations, parties) and protection of the appellation. Prosecco is a drink-now sparkling wine and needs no ageing.
slides.0.title: 🌍 Italian Grapes Around the World
slides.0.subtitle: The global journey of Sangiovese, Nebbiolo and Barbera
slides.1.title: 🌍 Taking Italian Grapes Global — Four Challenges
slides.1.content:
Compared with the global success of French grapes, Italian varieties face bigger obstacles abroad — strong terroir dependence, clonal complexity, the consumer knowledge barrier and the need for long ageing are the four core challenges; yet Sangiovese, Barbera and Prosecco already have success stories

🍇 Challenges Inherent in the Grapes

Extreme terroir dependence: Nebbiolo and Sangiovese are extremely demanding of geology and climate and rarely reach the same quality outside Piemonte/Tuscany; Nebbiolo is still centred on Piemonte

Clonal complexity: Sangiovese has dozens of registered clones that differ greatly; each Nebbiolo area has its own selections; growers abroad who pick the wrong clone fail

Contradictory personalities: high acid + high tannin are hard to enjoy before ageing, so first impressions are poor and marketing is difficult

📊 Marketing Challenges

A high knowledge barrier: "Chianti Classico Gran Selezione" is complicated vs "Cabernet Sauvignon", known worldwide; Italian grapes need a lot of consumer education

The need for long ageing: Nebbiolo, Aglianico and others need years of ageing, putting pressure on estates' cash flow and clashing with the New World's "drink now" market

Strong competitors: Bordeaux and Burgundy varieties went global long ago, leaving Italian grapes at a latecomer's disadvantage

slides.2.title: 🇺🇸 California — Sangiovese & Barbera
slides.2.content:
Brought by Italian immigrants in the late 19th century, revived by the Cal-Ital movement of the 1980s — Sangiovese is best represented by Atlas Peak (Napa, volcanic soils, high elevation); old-vine Barbera from the Sierra Foothills is sought after

🍷

Sangiovese in California

Key area: Atlas Peak (Napa, high-elevation volcanic soils, conditions closer to Tuscany)

Others: Dry Creek Valley (Sonoma, warm and fruity) / Sierra Foothills (traditional Italian-immigrant area)

Californian style: riper fruit, fuller body (plenty of sun), 14-15% alcohol, clear oak influence

Challenges: wrong early clone choices (high-yielding clones) + climates too hot, losing acidity

Producers: Seghesio / Atlas Peak Vineyards / Shafer "Firebreak"

🍇

Barbera in California

Old-vine treasure: Amador County (Sierra Foothills), where some old vines planted by Italian immigrants survive

Others: Central Valley (bulk everyday wine) / Paso Robles (modern oaked style)

Style: keeps its core high acidity, fruity (blackberry, black cherry), 13.5-15% alcohol

Market: a popular pairing in Italian restaurants; old-vine versions are sought after by enthusiasts

slides.3.title: 🇺🇸 California — Nebbiolo & the Cal-Ital Movement
slides.3.content:
The Cal-Ital movement's biggest challenge — Nebbiolo is the hardest grape to transplant; California has yet to match Barolo/Barbaresco quality, with differences in climate and microclimate at the heart of the problem

🍷 Nebbiolo in California

Area planted: tiny, with no commercial scale yet

Main sites: Spring Mountain (high-elevation Napa) / Westside (Paso Robles, limestone) / Ballard Canyon (Santa Barbara, ocean influence)

Biggest challenge: too hot → overripeness → loss of the elegance of Barolo/Barbaresco

Missing microclimate: Piemonte's autumn fogs (nebbia) delay harvest and preserve acidity — California cannot copy this

Clone problem: the right clones (Lampia/Michet/Rosé) are rare in California; most plantings use inferior clones

Conclusion: Barolo/Barbaresco quality has not yet been matched

🌟 The Cal-Ital Movement in Summary

Origins (1980s): a group of Italophile Californian growers began planting Italian varieties, known as the "Cal-Ital" movement

Pioneers: Robert Pepi (Sangiovese pioneer) / Atlas Peak Vineyards / Seghesio (Sangiovese + Barbera)

✅ Successes: Sangiovese (high quality at Atlas Peak) / Barbera (old vines in Amador County)

❌ Not yet successful: Nebbiolo / Sagrantino / Aglianico (highly terroir-dependent)

Key to success: the right climate + soil + clone; simply planting the grape does not reproduce Italian quality

slides.4.title: 🇦🇺 Australia — King Valley, a Testing Ground for Italian Grapes
slides.4.content:
The wine legacy of Australia's Italian immigrants — King Valley in Victoria is Australia's centre for Italian varieties, where families of Italian descent have passed down vineyards for generations, and Sangiovese and Barbera now show consistent quality

🏔️ King Valley (Victoria) — Home Base for Italian Varieties

After the Second World War many Italian immigrants grew tobacco here, later switching to vines and planting varieties from home. Now the stronghold of Italian varieties in Australia, its large elevation range and wide day-night swings help preserve acidity. Producers: Pizzini, Dal Zotto (families of Italian descent); in Victoria, Chalmers is known for introducing many Italian varieties. Main grapes: Sangiovese / Barbera / Nebbiolo / Arneis / Pinot Grigio.

🌡️ Adelaide Hills & McLaren Vale (South Australia)

Adelaide Hills (cool, high elevation): the most elegant Sangiovese, closest to the Italian originals. McLaren Vale (warm): fruity, full Sangiovese in a modern style. Producer: Coriole (McLaren Vale, Australia's Sangiovese pioneer in the 1980s).

📊 Italian Varieties in Australia Today

✅ Successes: Sangiovese + Barbera (a steady market, popular in Italian restaurants, a King Valley speciality). ❌ Challenge: Nebbiolo (too much sun, mostly overripe, not yet a commercial success). Character: Australia leans to a "New World" style (explosive fruit, clear oak), and the overall scale is still niche.

slides.5.title: 🇦🇷 Argentina — High-Altitude Heritage & the Great Bonarda Confusion
slides.5.content:
One of the South American countries with the most Italian immigrants (an estimated majority of the population has Italian ancestry) — high-altitude Mendoza preserves Barbera's acidity; but DNA shows that Argentina's "Bonarda" is actually Douce Noir from Savoie in France, not the Italian Bonarda!

🏔️ Barbera & Sangiovese in Argentina

History: from the late 19th century large numbers of Italian immigrants brought grapes from home

Main areas: Mendoza's Maipú/Luján de Cuyo (900-1,200 m) / San Juan (hotter)

High-altitude advantage: wide day-night swings preserve Barbera's acidity

Style: intense black fruit, 13.5-15% alcohol, some aged in French oak

Challenge: Malbec dominates the market → Italian grapes are hard to promote and little known

🧬 Bonarda (= Douce Noir): The DNA Revelation

Key finding: Argentina's "Bonarda" is neither Piemonte's Bonarda nor the Croatina called Bonarda in Oltrepò Pavese!

DNA research: Argentine Bonarda = Douce Noir from Savoie in France (called Charbono in California)

Area planted: one of Argentina's most planted red grapes after Malbec, on a large scale

Style: deep purple, explosive fruit (black fruit and spice), soft tannins, easy-drinking

Positioning: an affordable everyday red

Significance: long taken for an Italian grape until DNA research revealed the truth

slides.6.title: 🌍 Italian Grapes in Other Countries
slides.6.content:
From Brazil to South Africa, from New Zealand to Mexico — many countries grow Italian varieties, but most are still at a small experimental stage and have not yet reached commercial success

🇧🇷 Brazil — Rio Grande do Sul
One of the South American countries with the most Italian immigrants, with Serra Gaúcha as the main area. Main grapes: Barbera / a little Sangiovese. Challenges: a humid climate makes ripening difficult, quality is uneven and the market is mainly domestic.
🇿🇦 South Africa — Stellenbosch
Sangiovese is planted on a very small area, tried by a few estates such as Fairview and Neil Ellis. Style: fruity and full-bodied, but lacking the minerality and complexity of the Italian originals. Still a niche experiment.
🇳🇿 New Zealand — Hawke's Bay
A little Sangiovese and a tiny amount of Nebbiolo. The cool maritime climate preserves acidity, but humidity in the growing season makes ripening a challenge. Quality is not yet consistent, and growers are still searching for suitable sites.
🇲🇽 Mexico — Valle de Guadalupe
Small experimental plantings of Sangiovese / Nebbiolo in Baja California. The climate is too hot and dry, and no suitable microclimate for Italian varieties has yet been found. The conclusion so far: heat is the biggest obstacle, and higher sites are needed.
slides.7.title: 🍾 Prosecco — The Legend of an Italian Grape Gone Global
slides.7.content:
The perfect pairing of the Glera grape + the Charmat method — Prosecco is the greatest global success story of an Italian grape, with annual production in the hundreds of millions of bottles, far beyond Champagne, making it one of the world's best-selling sparkling wines

💶 Product Strengths

Grape: Glera (its official name since 2009). Charmat method (second fermentation in sealed tanks, faster and cheaper than the Champagne method). Style: light and fruity, off-dry (Extra Dry/Brut), low alcohol (about 11%), easy to understand. Affordable prices, precisely aimed at the mass market.

📣 Successful Marketing

Naming: "Prosecco" has three syllables and is easier than "Champagne" to pronounce and remember across languages. Occasions: "celebration + aperitivo + party", not competing with Champagne at formal dinners. The Aperol Spritz effect: Prosecco + Aperol + soda became one of the world's most popular cocktails, driving an explosion in sales.

🔒 Protecting the Appellation

2009: Prosecco became a DOC + DOCG (Conegliano Valdobbiadene), stopping imitations worldwide. Quality ladder: Superiore di Cartizze and Rive (steep vineyards in specific villages) > Conegliano Valdobbiadene and Asolo DOCGs > Prosecco DOC, a successful differentiation. The Consorzio (appellation body) promotes it heavily, sponsoring music festivals and bar education worldwide.

Hundreds of millions of bottles/year
Far beyond Champagne

slides.8.title: 🔍 Italian Originals vs New World Styles
slides.8.content:
🌍 Do Grapes Change When They Leave Italy?

The same grape in a different terroir almost always produces a different style. The core issue: the New World's abundant sun + warm climate ripens grapes faster with riper fruit, while Italy's high acid + minerality + complexity needs specific terroirs and is hard to replicate.

🇮🇹 Italian Original Style

Acidity + tannin: high (the terroir protects the grape's DNA)

Minerality: strong (specific volcanic/limestone/tuff soils)

Built for ageing: needs long waiting, with complexity emerging after ageing

Alcohol: low to medium (12.5-14%)

Terroir-led: the same grape varies greatly by village and plot

Complex maturity: hard to enjoy young, needs patience

🌏 New World Italian-Grape Style

Fruit: riper and easier to drink (plenty of sun, drink-now friendly)

Body: fuller (ripened in heat, high anthocyanins)

Oak: more evident (high use of new American/French oak)

Alcohol: higher (14-16%)

Variety-led: highlights varietal fruit, reducing site differences

Drinking window: earlier, suiting New World drinking habits

Replicated
Sangiovese / Barbera
Hard to replicate

slides.9.title: 🎓 Key Takeaways
slides.9.points.0: ✓ Four challenges in taking Italian grapes global: strong terroir dependence, clonal complexity (dozens of Sangiovese clones), a high consumer knowledge barrier and the need for long ageing
slides.9.points.1: ✓ California: Sangiovese is best represented by Napa's Atlas Peak (high-elevation volcanic soils); old-vine Barbera from Amador County is sought after; Nebbiolo has not yet succeeded
slides.9.points.2: ✓ The Cal-Ital movement (1980s): successfully introduced Sangiovese/Barbera, but Nebbiolo/Aglianico remain hard to replicate because they depend so heavily on terroir
slides.9.points.3: ✓ Australia's King Valley: where Italian immigrants settled after the Second World War, Sangiovese/Barbera now show consistent quality; Nebbiolo is mostly overripe because of the strong sun
slides.9.points.4: ✓ Argentina: high-altitude Mendoza preserves Barbera's acidity; the widely planted "Bonarda" has been shown by DNA to be Douce Noir (California's Charbono), not an Italian grape
slides.9.points.5: ✓ Other countries (Brazil/South Africa/New Zealand/Mexico) are at a small experimental stage, held back mainly by humid or overly hot climates
slides.9.points.6: ✓ Prosecco (the Glera grape) is the greatest global success of an Italian grape, producing hundreds of millions of bottles a year, far beyond Champagne; DOC/DOCG status in 2009 protected Italy's exclusive right to the name
slides.9.points.7: ✓ Prosecco's three keys to success: affordable prices + an easy-drinking style (low barrier) + a simple name (pronounceable in every language)
slides.9.points.8: ✓ New World styles of Italian grapes: riper fruit, fuller body, more evident oak, slightly higher alcohol, earlier drinking; the Italian originals win on minerality, structure and complexity with age
